source.title: Efficient Unlearning through Maximizing Relearning Convergence Delay

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests relearning after unlearning, but in image-classification and text-to-image generation settings rather than LLMs.
record.gate_note: The study fine-tunes unlearned models on forgotten data to measure relearning. The generation attack uses Adam to relearn targeted NSFW concepts, and the classification setup trains on the training-forgetting set. Neither tests unrelated or loosely related examples, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompting-only recovery. Other reported unlearning and retention metrics are not included as recovery rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs relearning attacks on unlearned models: fine-tuning on the forgotten data for image classifiers, and fine-tuning toward the original model's outputs for Stable Diffusion. It also proposes IEU as a method that resists relearning. Its relearning-convergence-delay (RCD) results bear on B and F, but only outside LLMs, so the tranche is T3. For classifiers the relearning data is the whole 30–50% forget set, measured against a retrained (never-trained-on-forget) model. For SD the relearning target is the original model's predictions (distillation). Neither setup is a small or unrelated relearning set.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but it understates how general the claim is. The abstract claims IEU resists relearning in both classification and generation tasks. The conclusion says IEU, especially with Noisy, improves resistance to data recovery. The authors' own Stable Diffusion results contradict this for generation, and they say so in three places. Section 6.2 says IEU variants, particularly Noisy, relearn faster and are more susceptible under Adam. Section 11.3.3 calls all methods similarly vulnerable. The Limitations section says the framework is less effective under Adam relearning and calls Adam-specific resistance future work. The authors also say that scaling to language and graph domains is unsolved.
record.recipe_differences: IEU combines gradient ascent and noisy regularization/weight reinitialization in image-classification and diffusion models; it does not test the cited LLM unlearning recipes or LLM recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports different resistance behavior for gradient-descent classification relearning versus Adam-based Stable Diffusion relearning. Classification RCD comparisons also vary with step-size; smaller step-sizes reduce score differentiation. In the Noisy ablation, excessive noise harms utility and large α reduces forgetting effectiveness.
record.peer_reviewed: 2026 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition- FINDINGS Track (CVPRF)
record.problems: The experiments use vision and diffusion models, not LLMs. The classification attack relearns on the training-forgetting set, and the diffusion attack targets NSFW concepts; neither evaluates a small unrelated or loosely related relearning set. The paper notes that the proposed approach is less effective with Adam. Some classification RCD results are presented in plots and aggregate prose rather than a fully enumerated numeric table.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying recovery result was omitted. Classification tables of accuracy, MIA, retention, nudity, and FID were not entered as separate rows because they do not measure recovery under the attacks in the tested versions.

untested.parts: Not tested. There are no LLMs and no simple-attack battery. Class-wise forgetting brings forgotten-class test accuracy to 0 while keeping retain accuracy, but the only attack is relearning (version B), and nothing tests whether simple attacks fail.

Relearning with a small, unrelated or loosely related set, or with a subset of forgotten items tested on held-out ones. No LLM setting. The study uses the full forget set, or distillation from the original model.
No activation-direction ablation and no analysis of blocked access versus deletion.
No prompting-only recovery (rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, in-context information).
Resistance to internal edits, quantization or prompting attacks; resistance to small or unrelated relearning sets; any LLM setting.

missing.what: Per-method RCD values with the retraining (never-trained) reference: Retraining 44.91, FT 4.32, RL 30.82, SCRUB 8.37 (from the caption); SALUN 42.01 (panel mapping inferred). This is the only numeric comparison of unlearned vs never-trained relearning speed. The figure's model and dataset are not stated.

IEU variants' RCD in the same figure: w/GA 10.95, w/Noisy 31.05, w/GA+Noisy 31.05 (panel mapping inferred from extracted text), vs retraining 44.91 and baselines FT 4.32, SCRUB 8.37, RL 30.82, SALUN 42.01.

Trade-off of RCD against retention accuracy across IEU α and c settings on ViT/CIFAR-100: more noise raises RCD at a small accuracy cost, and weaker gradient ascent lowers resistance. Values are plotted only.

record.verdict_notes: The record's version ids V1–V6 map to A–F by content (V1 unlearning works, V2 fine-tuning recovery, V3 internal edits, V4 quantization, V5 prompting, V6 counter-methods). Every row R1–R10 has a fix with declared ids. Changes from the earlier verdict: (1) Split missing[].versions 'B, F' into one entry per version, since a combined string is not a declared id. (2) R10 now links to B only. The earlier [B, F] link with state 'observed' would show F's resistance as observed, when for F it is absent. The F challenge now rests on R3–R9 plus Sec 11.3.3 text. (3) Added a B limits_scope label for RL, SALUN and the IEU Noisy variants. Their Fig 5 RCD is close to retraining, which a mixed-results reading requires; the earlier verdict labelled only FT/SCRUB. (4) Corrected the problem texts for R3/R4/R8 and the authors_conclusion: Section 6.2, not only the Limitations, admits IEU relearns faster under Adam. (5) Reworded A's untested parts, since class-wise forgetting does reach 0 accuracy on forgotten classes. Fig 5's panel-to-value mapping for SALUN and the IEU variants is inferred from scrambled PDF text. Only Retraining, FT, RL and SCRUB are fixed by the caption. States kept: R3/R4/R7/R8 absent, R5/R9 reversed. All differences are under 5% with no uncertainty reported, and the appendix calls them comparable. Sec 6.2's wording would let R4 be read as weakly reversed. This is a vision/diffusion study, not LLMs, so all links are cross-domain (T3) and weak evidence for the LLM-framed claim. RCD measures relearning speed on the full forget set, not recovery after a small relearning set. The F verdicts depend on the relearning optimizer (SGD vs Adam) and the step size. No instructions to the reader were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test whether an LLM method brings targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance while preserving general ability and whether the listed simple attacks then fail.
Tests relearning by fine-tuning on forgotten training data or NSFW concepts, but does not test a small, unrelated, loosely related, or explicitly limited subset relearning set.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language-switching, or in-context-only recovery test.
Tests IEU's resistance to relearning, but not resistance to the other listed attacks or in LLMs.

rows.measure: RCDGD, a measure of relearning convergence delay
rows.baseline: Retraining model is described as the ideal-unlearning reference; specific numeric comparison not stated in this aggregate result.
rows.value: Authors report that IEU methods, particularly those with Noisy, achieve high RCDGD; retraining is highest across nearly all configurations, while FT and SCRUB are among the weakest.
rows.note: Aggregate prose across multiple separately plotted settings, not a per-model numeric result. High RCDGD means slower relearning; the paper describes IEU as comparatively resistant in these gradient-descent classification experiments.
rows.check: The record's ids V2/V6 map to B/F. This row aggregates all methods. Supplement Fig 5 gives numbers the row lacks. The caption fixes retraining 44.91, FT 4.32, RL 30.82 and SCRUB 8.37. Panel mapping inferred from the extracted text gives SALUN 42.01, IEU w/GA 10.95, and 31.05 for both IEU w/Noisy and w/GA+Noisy. For B, FT and SCRUB relearn far faster than the never-trained reference, while RL, SALUN and the Noisy variants come close to it. For F, IEU's resistance stays below retraining and is no higher than RL. Relearning uses the whole forget set for 100 SGD epochs. Fig 5's model and dataset are not stated. The row should be split per method.

conditions.value: relearned outputs compared visually with original SD outputs

rows.value: Authors report that relearned outputs closely resemble those from original SD; they also describe the relearning scores across methods as comparable.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative report; Figure 22 displays examples but does not give per-method numerical outcomes.
rows.check: The record's V2/V6 map to B here. The evidence is qualitative: relearned outputs closely resemble the original SD (Fig 22, Sec 11.3.3), and no numeric recovery measure is given. The relearning target is the original SD's own noise predictions (Adam, lr 1e-5, step count not stated), not a small relearning set. There is no never-trained reference, so the row shows that recovery happens, not that it beats learning from scratch. The row also implies IEU gives no protection (F absent). It is not linked to F because a single state cannot be 'observed' for B and 'absent' for F. The F label rests on R3–R9 and this text.

source_check.notes: Table 3 and Fig 5 are flattened. Table 3's order checks out against the text. Fig 5's model, dataset and forgetting scenario are not stated, and only the Retraining/FT/RL/SCRUB values are fixed by its caption. The abstract claims resistance in generation, but the authors' own SD results and the Sec 12 limitation contradict it.

statements.correction: 2604.09391: ResNet-50/ViT on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet, SGD relearning on the full forget set for 100 epochs. Fig 5: FT RCD 4.32 and SCRUB 8.37 vs retraining 44.91, RL 30.82. Inferred panel mapping: SALUN 42.01, IEU Noisy variants 31.05.
statements.problem: It cites this study's R1 but says nothing about the study. Its conditions list (ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10/SVHN/Imagenette) leaves out this study's setting. R1 is a mixed aggregate: FT and SCRUB relearn fast, while IEU Noisy, SALUN and RL sit closer to retraining.
SCRUB 8.37 vs retraining 44.91 matches the Fig 5 caption, and so does the SGD, full-forget-set description (Sec 10.1.4). The numbers come from the caption, not from R1's prose value.

statements.correction: SD v1.4, Adam lr 1e-5: every IEU variant is 0.9-4.5% below its vanilla method, and the authors call the scores comparable and the methods similarly vulnerable. Classification (Fig 5, SGD): IEU Noisy 31.05, about RL's 30.82, far above FT 4.32 and SCRUB 8.37, below SALUN 42.01 and retraining 44.91.
statements.problem: The SD Table 3 numbers are right. But in image classification IEU does slow relearning: Noisy 31.05 vs FT 4.32 (IEU's own alpha=1, c=0 base) and SCRUB 8.37. So 'slows relearning little or not at all' does not fit there. The Noisy 31.05 panel mapping is inferred.
The IEU range of 1-4.5% is right (the lowest is 0.94%, SALUN w/Noisy). The similar-vulnerability wording is in Sec 11.3.3, and the abstract claims resistance in generation tasks.

statements.correction: 2604.09391: in classification, SGD relearning gives IEU Noisy RCD 31.05 vs FT 4.32 (Fig 5). In SD v1.4, Adam relearning gives every IEU variant 0.9-4.5% below vanilla (R3 526.653 vs 538.022; R9 506.544 vs 530.431). Sec 6.2 and Sec 12 say IEU is less effective under Adam relearning. The optimizer is confounded with task and model.
statements.problem: It cites R1, R3 and R9 but says nothing about this study. Those rows do bear on attack-configuration sensitivity: IEU resists SGD relearning in classification but not Adam relearning in SD, which the authors attribute to Adam dynamics.
